{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
In [[axiomatic set theory]], a mathematical discipline, a '''morass''' is an infinite combinatorial structure, used to create "large" structures from a "small" number of "small" approximations.  They were invented by [[Ronald Jensen]] for his proof that cardinal transfer theorems hold under the [[axiom of constructibility]].  A far less complex but equivalent variant known as a '''simplified morass''' was introduced by Velleman, and the term morass is now often used to mean these simpler structures.

== Overview ==
Whilst it is possible to define so-called gap-''n'' morasses for ''n''&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;1, they are so complex that focus is usually restricted to the gap-1 case, except for specific applications.  The "gap" is essentially the cardinal difference between the size of the "small approximations" used and the size of the ultimate structure.

A (gap-1) morass on an [[uncountable]] [[regular cardinal]] ''κ'' (also called a '''(''κ'',''1'')-morass''') consists of a [[tree (set theory)|tree]] of height ''κ''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, with the top level having ''κ''<sup>+</sup>-many nodes.  The nodes are taken to be [[Ordinal number|ordinals]], and functions {{pi}} between these ordinals are associated to the edges in the tree order.  It is required that the ordinal structure of the top level nodes be "built up" as the direct limit of the ordinals in the branch to that node by the maps π, so the lower level nodes can be thought of as approximations to the (larger) top level node. 
A long list of further axioms is imposed to have this happen in a particularly "nice" way.<ref>K. Devlin.  ''Constructibility''. Springer, Berlin, 1984.</ref><ref name=V82>{{cite journal | last=Velleman | first=Daniel J. | title=Morasses, diamond, and forcing | zbl=0521.03034 | journal=Ann. Math. Logic | volume=23 | pages=199–281 | year=1982 | doi=10.1016/0003-4843(82)90005-5 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Variants and equivalents ==
Velleman<ref name=V82/> and [[Saharon Shelah|Shelah]] and Stanley<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Shelah | first1=S. | last2=Stanley | first2=L. | title=S-forcing, I: A "black box" theorem for morasses, with applications: Super-Souslin trees and generalizing Martin's axiom | journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]] | volume=43 | year=1982 | pages=185&ndash;224 | doi=10.1007/BF02761942 | doi-access=free}}</ref> independently developed [[forcing axiom]]s equivalent to the existence of morasses, to facilitate their use by non-experts.  Going further, Velleman<ref>{{cite journal | last=Velleman | first=Dan | title=Simplified morasses | zbl=0575.03035 | journal=Journal of Symbolic Logic | volume=49 | number=1 | pages=257–271 | year=1984 | doi=10.2307/2274108 }}</ref> showed that the existence of morasses is equivalent to [[Morass (set theory)#Simplified morass|simplified morasses]], which are vastly simpler structures.  However, the only known construction of a simplified morass in [[Kurt Gödel|Gödel's]] [[constructible universe]] is by means of morasses, so the original notion retains interest.

Other variants on morasses, generally with added structure, have also appeared over the years.  These include ''universal morasses,''<ref>K. Devlin.  ''Aspects of Constructibility'', Lecture Notes in Mathematics 354, Springer, Berlin, 1973.</ref> whereby every subset of ''κ'' is built up through the branches of the morass, ''mangroves,''<ref>{{cite journal | first1=A. |last1=Brooke-Taylor | first2=S. | last2=Friedman | title=Large cardinals and gap-1 morasses | arxiv=0801.1912| journal=Annals of Pure and Applied Logic | zbl=1165.03033 | volume=159 | number=1-2 | pages=71–99 | year=2009 | doi=10.1016/j.apal.2008.10.007 }}</ref> which are morasses stratified into levels (''mangals'') at which every branch must have a node, and ''quagmires''.<ref>{{cite book | last=Kanamori | first=Akihiro | chapter=Morasses in combinatorial set theory | zbl=0525.03036 | title=Surveys in set theory | series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series | volume=87 | pages=167–196 | year=1983 | editor1-last=Mathias | editor1-first=A.R.D. | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=0-521-27733-7 }}</ref>

==Simplified morass==

Velleman <ref>D. Velleman.  Simplified Morasses, ''Journal of Symbolic Logic'' '''49''', No. 1 (1984),  pp 257&ndash;271.</ref> defined gap-1 ''simplified morasses'' which are much simpler than gap-1 morasses, and showed that the existence of gap-1 morasses is equivalent to the existence of gap-1 simplified morasses.

Roughly speaking: a (''κ'',1)-'''simplified morass''' '''M''' = < φ<sup>→</sup>, F<sup>⇒</sup> > contains a sequence φ<sup>→</sup> = <&nbsp;φ<sub>''β''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''β''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''κ''&nbsp;> of ordinals such that φ<sub>β</sub>&nbsp;<&nbsp;''κ'' for ''β''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''κ'' and φ<sub>''κ''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''κ''<sup>+</sup>, and a double sequence ''F''<sup>⇒</sup> =&nbsp;<&nbsp;''F''<sub>''α'',''β''</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;α&nbsp;<&nbsp;''β''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''κ''&nbsp;> where ''F''<sub>''α'',''β''</sub> are collections of monotone mappings from φ<sub>''α''</sub> to φ<sub>''β''</sub> for ''α''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''β'' &nbsp;≤&nbsp;''κ'' with specific (easy but important) conditions.

Velleman's clear definition can be found in,<ref>D. Velleman.  Simplified Morasses, ''Journal of Symbolic Logic'' '''49''', No. 1 (1984), pp 257&ndash;271.</ref> where he also constructed (ω<sub>0</sub>,1) simplified morasses in [[ZFC]]. In <ref>D. Velleman. Simplified Gap-2 Morasses, ''Annals of Pure and Applied Logic'' '''34''', (1987), pp 171–208.</ref> he gave similar simple definitions for gap-2 ''simplified morasses'', and in <ref>D. Velleman. Gap-2 Morasses of Height ω<sub>0</sub>, ''Journal of Symbolic Logic'' '''52''', (1987), pp 928–938.</ref> he constructed (ω<sub>0</sub>,2) simplified morasses in [[ZFC]].

'''Higher gap''' simplified morasses for any ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1 were defined by Morgan <ref>Ch. Morgan. ''The Equivalence of Morasses and Simplified Morasses in the Finite Gap Case'', PhD.Thesis, Merton College, UK, 1989.</ref> and Szalkai.<ref>I. Szalkai. ''Higher Gap Simplified Morasses and Combinatorial Applications'', PhD-Thesis (in Hungarian), ELTE, Budapest, 1991. English abstract: 
http://math.uni-pannon.hu/~szalkai/Szalkai-1991d-MorassAbst-.pdf</ref><ref>I. Szalkai. An Inductive Definition of Higher Gap Simplified Morasses, ''Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen'' '''58''' (2001), pp 605–634. http://math.uni-pannon.hu/~szalkai/Szalkai-2001a-IndMorass.pdf</ref>

Roughly speaking: a (''κ'',''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)-'''simplified morass''' (of Szalkai) '''M''' = <&nbsp;''M''<sup>→</sup>,&nbsp;''F''<sup>⇒</sup>&nbsp;> contains a sequence ''M''<sup>→</sup> = <&nbsp;''M''<sub>''β''</sub> : ''β''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''κ''&nbsp;> of  (<&nbsp;''κ'',''n'')-simplified morass-like structures for ''β''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''κ'' and ''M''<sub>''κ''</sub> a (''κ''<sup>+</sup>,''n'') -simplified morass, and a double  sequence F<sup>⇒</sup> =  <&nbsp;''F''<sub>α,β</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''α''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''β''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;κ&nbsp;> where ''F''<sub>''α'',''β''</sub> are collections of mappings from ''M''<sub>''α''</sub> to ''M''<sub>''β''</sub> for ''α''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''β''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''κ'' with specific conditions.
